messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: C++-11 features for unit tests?
parts: Anyone care if the tests have C++-11 features? I'm wanting to use default template parameters for functions. This would make testing the distributions a lot easier and we might have a real chance at testing the distributions with the bounds included.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++-11 features for unit tests?
parts:
On 11/15/12 11:39 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Anyone care if the tests have C++-11 features? I'm wanting to use default template parameters for functions. This would
> make testing the distributions a lot easier and we might have a real chance at testing the distributions with the bounds
> included.

It's OK by me.

It won't get in the way of an eventual CRAN-compatible
RStan (not that I've ever cared about that).

If we just give up on CRAN (or they start accepting
more modern code), we could use C++11 features in
the rest of Stan.

All the compilers that could handle our templates could
handle the C++11 features we were using for default
error policies in template functions.

- Bob

On Thursday, November 15, 2012 11:39:14 PM UTC-5, Daniel Lee wrote:
Anyone care if the tests have C++-11 features? I'm wanting to use default template parameters for functions. This would make testing the distributions a lot easier and we might have a real chance at testing the distributions with the bounds included.

This seems to be a bit more problematic on clang than I would have guessed. I didn't notice before because --std wasn't actually getting set on linux until now.

First, there is an issue where clang does not support __float128

http://llvm.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=13530

but I got around that by doing -D__STRICT_ANSI__, as suggested. Then, I get an error in test-unit

I just tried test-unit with Clang's version of the C++ standard library. To do this, you need to install it and add

somewhere like make/os_*. But we get errors

Upon further review, these are due to using the .real() method in eigendecompositions. To me, things like

Eigen::EigenSolver<matrix_v> solver(m);
return solver.eigenvectors().real();

are problematic. Either m is symmetric, in which case the calling function should have used the _sym variants, which in turn utilize SelfAdjointEigenSolver, or m is not symmetric in which case just returning the real part is generally not the right answer. I think there are cases where all the eigenvalues happen to be real even though the matrix is asymmetric, but they are not likely to occur when m is a matrix_v and it is not like we are verifying that anyway.

Side note: Another argument against hard-coding vars as doubles is that we can't support densities that involve complex numbers. Not that there are millions of users clamoring for complex number support, but there will probably be one eventually.

Then, there are some parts like this

Eigen::SelfAdjointEigenSolver<matrix_v> solver(m,Eigen::EigenvaluesOnly);
return solver.eigenvalues().real();

where the .real() is just unnecessary because the .eigenvalues() of a SelfAdjointEigenSolver are real by construction.

If I fix all that, then test-unit only has a few (unique) errors, all of which seem to be due to io or gm (full log attached).

My linear algebra's wobbly at best -- I'm happy to

results.

I see that you're using SelfAdjointEigenSolver.  With that,
we could either test for symmetry (within some tolerance)
or just doc it as working on the replicated lower-triangular
matrix (which is what it does according to its doc).  I'm
happy with either solution.

I don't think Eigen checks for SelfAdjointness, but Stan probably should. The cost of a symmetry check is going to be tiny relative to the cost of auto-diffing a tridiagonalization and a sequence of QR factorizations. It might even be the case that a JacobiSVD of a parameterized symmetric matrix is faster than a SelfAdjointEigenSolver when the auto-diffing is taken into account.

Ben

> case that a JacobiSVD of a parameterized symmetric matrix is faster than a SelfAdjointEigenSolver when the auto-diffing
> is taken into account.

This is different behavior rather than dropping
a check. It's what Eigen does.

Eigen doesn't check that the matrix coming in is
symmetric. In fact, it guarantees it won't look
above the diagonal, so all that can be empty (or
used for something else as their doc says).

So there are two different methods, really:

eigenvalues_sym(matrix,...);

eigenvalues_low_tri_self_adjoint(matrix,...);

First would test for symmetry in the matrix but only use
the lower triangular part. Second would only use the lower
triangular part.

- Bob

On Thursday, November 22, 2012 2:47:51 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
I'm happy to get rid of eigen decompositions for
asymmetric matrices and change the doc.

The only reason I can see to not get rid of it is because it is already there. But I doubt anyone is using it because it doesn't really make sense. It is rare to see eigenvalues being calculated in statistical models, rarer that the matrix in question is not positive definite, even rarer that the matrix is not symmetric, and I've never seen a statistical model where the relevant quantity is the real part of complex eigenvalues.

I'm not sure we should just disappear exposed functions. Can the parser be configured to give a deprecation message / suggested alternative if eig() appears in a .stan file?

Ben

to match the doc and treat outcomes as ranging from 1 to N instead

but I could create a set of signatures to check during parsing.
